description: Not independently attested in Zulu tradition. No 'wolf giant' appears in Bantu oral records; wolves are absent from sub-Saharan Africa. The record likely conflates the Zulu river-goddess Mamlambo (a serpentine water spirit) with foreign wolf motifs. Zulu myth features sky spirits like Umvelinqangi and the shape-shifting Nomkhubulwane, but no wolf-beings.
source: Berglund, 'Zulu Thought-Patterns and Symbolism'; Callaway, 'Religious System of the Amazulu'; Wikipedia: Zulu traditional religion
research_notes: Wolves do not exist in southern Africa; Zulu myth has no wolf figures. The 'Wolf Giant' appears to be a fabricated entry conflating Mamlambo (goddess of rivers, serpentine) with non-African wolf mythology. Country/culture attribution is South Africa but the being is unattested.

description: Not independently attested in Botswana or Mapuche tradition. Mapuche (Chile/Argentina) mythology features the fox-like trickster Colocolo and the shapeshifting Kalku, but no wolf trickster. Wolves are absent from both southern Africa and Patagonia. The record misattributes a South American culture to Botswana and invents a wolf figure where none exists.
source: Bacigalupo, 'Shamans of the Foye Tree'; Wikipedia: Mapuche religion; Botswana mythology surveys
research_notes: Mapuche are indigenous to Chile/Argentina, not Botswana. No wolf species exist in either region. The entry duplicates 'wolftrickstermapuche-chile' and 'wolftrickstermapuche-mexico' aliases, confirming fabrication. Closest real analogue: Mapuche Colocolo (fox trickster) or Kalku (sorcerer/shapeshifter).

description: Not independently attested in Zimbabwean tradition. The description matches Laotian 'Moon Bear' animist beliefs (lunar cycles, rice agriculture, nocturnal protection), not Shona or Ndebele folklore. Zimbabwe has no native bear species. The record misplaces a Laotian deity into southern Africa, likely via erroneous cultural conflation.
source: Laotian animism studies; Shona mythology (Gelfand, 'The Genuine Shona'); Zimbabwean folklore surveys
research_notes: Description text explicitly states 'moon bear deity of Laotian animism' and details Laotian agricultural cycles. Zimbabwe has no bears; Shona spirits include Mhondoro (lion ancestors) and Nyaminyami (river serpent), not bear deities. Real analogue: Laotian Moon Bear spirit; Zimbabwean correction: none — this is a misplaced Laotian entry.

description: Attested in Bhutanese folk tradition as protective water spirits linked to frog/toad deities of paddy fields. Bhutanese Buddhism incorporates pre-Buddhist nature spirits (lü, klu) guarding water and agriculture. The toad spirit guards fields and irrigation, consistent with Himalayan 'lu' (naga) traditions. Specific named 'Toad Water-Spirit' not in canonical texts but fits the genre.
source: Bhutanese folklore collections; 'Culture of Bhutan' (Wikipedia); Himalayan Buddhist spirit lore (lü/klu)
research_notes: Bhutanese tradition includes frog/toad spirits protecting fields and water. The generic 'toad water-spirit' is plausible but not a specific named figure in major texts. Related to Chimi Lhakhang fertility rites and Drukpa Kunley narratives. Verified as genre-attested, not a specific named entity.

description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Baloch oral tradition (shahr, dastan) features heroes like Mir Chakar Rind, Hammal Jiand, and desert djinn (Mujna), but no turtle giants. Turtles are not prominent in arid Balochistan mythology. The record appears fabricated, possibly conflating Hindu Kurma avatar with Baloch culture.
source: Balochi folklore collections (Dashti, 'The Baloch and Their Neighbours'); Balochi oral literature surveys; Shahnameh Baloch references
research_notes: Balochistan is arid/mountainous; turtle myths are absent. Baloch epics focus on tribal heroes, desert spirits, and Islamic-influenced djinn. No 'turtle giant' in recorded dastans. Closest real analogue: Hindu Kurma (tortoise avatar of Vishnu) or Makara (crocodile/fish hybrid), but these are South Asian, not Baloch.

description: Airavata is the divine white elephant of Hindu myth, mount of Indra, born from the churning of the ocean of milk. Described with four tusks, seven trunks (or three heads/six tusks), pristine white skin. Guards Svarga's entrance, controls rain clouds. Appears in Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavad Gita (10.27), Puranas. Known as Erawan in Thai/Lao tradition, on royal flags.
source: Dalal, 'Hinduism: An Alphabetical Guide'; Bhagavad Gita 10.27; Ramayana; Vishnu Purana; Matsya Purana; Thai/Lao royal iconography
research_notes: Well-documented across Hindu, Buddhist, and Southeast Asian traditions. The record's country (India) and culture (India) are correct. Multiple textual sources from Vedic through Puranic periods. Thai/Lao Erawan is a direct cultural transmission.

description: Maha Sohona (Great Cemetery Demon) is a major demon in Sinhala Sri Lankan folklore, king of the Sanni Yakku (disease demons). He dwells in cremation grounds, devours corpses, and spreads plagues. Described as terrifying with red eyes, fangs, and a corpse-strewn form. Can be propitiated by rituals (thovil) but is ruthless. Documented by Wirz, Obeyesekere, and in Kandyan period texts.
source: Obeyesekere, 'The Work of the Devil'; Wirz, 'Exorcism in Sinhalese Buddhism'; Gananath Obeyesekere fieldwork; Sri Lankan demonology
research_notes: Well-attested in Sinhala exorcism tradition. The record's country (Sri Lanka) and culture (Sri Lanka) are correct. Central to Sanni Yakku system of 18 disease demons. Living tradition in thovil healing rituals.

description: Makara is the legendary aquatic hybrid of Hindu/Buddhist myth — crocodile forequarters, elephant trunk, fish tail, peacock feathers. Mount (vahana) of Ganga and Varuna; guardian of temple thresholds (torana). Appears from 2nd c. BCE (Besnagar pillar) across South/Southeast Asia. Zodiac sign Capricorn. Not specifically 'Bangladeshi' — pan-South Asian.
source: Makara iconography studies (Beer, 'Encyclopedia of Tibetan Symbols'); Hindu temple architecture; Buddhist art (Borobudur, Angkor, Sanchi); Sanskrit texts
research_notes: Pan-South/Southeast Asian, not unique to Bangladesh. Record's country attribution is narrow; culture should be 'South Asia' or 'Hindu/Buddhist'. Well-documented from Vedic to medieval periods across 10+ countries. Sri Lankan 'Makara' = dragon in Sinhala Buddhist art.

description: Manasa is the Hindu snake-goddess worshipped across Bengal for snakebite protection, fertility, prosperity. Daughter of Kashyapa (or Shiva in Mangalkavyas), sister of Vasuki, wife of Jaratkaru, mother of Astika. Central to Manasamangal Kavya (Bengali medieval epics). Worshipped via cactus branch, earthen pot, snake image; festival Nag Panchami. Cult rivals Shaivism; assimilated by 14th century.
source: Dimock, 'The Place of the Hidden Moon'; McDaniel, 'Offering Flowers, Feeding Skulls'; Chakravarty, 'Manasa'; Manasamangal Kavya (Vijay Gupta, Bipradas Pipilai); Bhattacharyya, 'Serpent as Folk-Deity in Bengal'
research_notes: Extensively documented in Bengali Mangalkavyas (13th–18th c.), Puranas, and living worship. Record correctly places her in India; the Bangladesh entry (manasa-bangladesh) is the same deity across the Bengal region. Source quality 'expert' for the tradition.

description: Manasa is the Hindu snake-goddess worshipped across Bengal for snakebite protection, fertility, prosperity. Daughter of Kashyapa, sister of Vasuki, wife of Jaratkaru, mother of Astika. Central to Manasamangal Kavya (Bengali medieval epics). Worshipped via cactus branch, earthen pot, snake image; festival Nag Panchami. Cult rivals Shaivism; assimilated by 14th century.
source: Banglapedia (Manasa entry); Dimock, 'The Place of the Hidden Moon'; McDaniel, 'Offering Flowers, Feeding Skulls'; Manasamangal Kavya; Bangladeshi folk worship studies
research_notes: Same deity as manasa-india; the Bengal region spans both countries. Record duplication reflects political borders, not cultural distinction. Well-documented in both nations. Attestation is for the shared Bengali tradition.

description: Matsya (Fish) is the first avatar of Vishnu in the Dashavatara. In Shatapatha Brahmana, a fish saves Manu from the great flood; later Puranas identify it as Vishnu. Matsya warns Manu, has him build a boat, tows it to Himalayas with Vedas, sages, seeds. In Bhagavata Purana, slays demon Hayagriva who stole the Vedas. Depicted as giant golden fish or half-Vishnu/half-fish. Embodies flood myth motif.
source: Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1; Matsya Purana; Bhagavata Purana; Mahabharata Vana Parva; Vishnu Purana; Agni Purana; Dalal, 'Hinduism: An Alphabetical Guide'
research_notes: Well-attested from Vedic (Shatapatha Brahmana) through Puranic literature. Record's country (India) and culture (India) correct. The 'forest-spirit' archetype in the record is erroneous — Matsya is a divine avatar, not a forest spirit.

description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Moose are not native to Balochistan (arid Pakistan/Iran/Afghanistan). Baloch oral tradition features tribal heroes (Mir Chakar Rind, Hammal Jiand), desert djinn (Mujna), and mountain spirits, but no moose giants. The record appears fabricated, possibly conflating North American moose mythology with Baloch culture.
source: Balochi folklore collections (Dashti); Balochistan fauna records; Balochi dastan surveys
research_notes: Moose (Alces alces) range is boreal Northern Hemisphere; absent from Balochistan. Baloch epics focus on desert/mountain landscapes, camels, horses, tribal warfare. No moose in any recorded dastan or shahr. Closest real analogue: Baloch mountain spirits or the heroic figure Mir Chakar Rind (associated with mountains), but no moose.

description: Not independently attested as 'Moppet' in Indian folklore. The description matches Arunachal Pradesh 'Yeti' variants (small hairy forest hominids) reported by Monpa, Sherdukpen, and other tribal groups. 'Moppet' appears to be an invented English name for local wild-man traditions (e.g., Miri 'Mande Barung', Mishmi 'Yeti' variants). Arunachal has numerous hominid cryptids but no canonical 'Moppet'.
source: Arunachal Pradesh tribal folklore (Monpa, Mishmi, Sherdukpen); Himalayan hominid cryptid surveys (Yeti variants); Indian cryptozoology literature
research_notes: 'Moppet' is not a local name; likely an AI-invented label. Arunachal has genuine wild-man traditions (Mande Barung, Yeti variants) but they are unnamed or have tribal names. The record's 'small hairy forest creature, regional yeti variant' is genre-accurate but the name 'Moppet' is fabricated. Real analogue: Arunachal wild-man / Mande Barung.

description: Mujna (or Mujina) is a desert djinn (jinn) in Pakistani Baloch/Sindhi folklore. Appears to lost travelers in the desert, grants wishes but demands payment (often tragic). Part of Islamic-influenced folk belief in Balochistan and Sindh. Similar to Persian 'Mujina' (badger-shapeshifter) but localized as a desert wish-granting spirit. Documented in regional folk collections and oral accounts.
source: Pakistani Baloch/Sindhi folklore collections; Islamic folk belief in South Asia (jinn traditions); regional oral narratives
research_notes: Attested in Pakistani desert folklore as a djinn figure. The name may relate to Persian 'mujina' (badger) but function is distinct. Record's country (Pakistan) and culture (Pakistan) are correct. Genre: Islamic folk belief / jinn lore, not pre-Islamic Baloch myth.

description: Lhamu are Tibetan-influenced shapeshifting spirits in Nepali Sherpa/Himalayan folklore. Appear as monks, travelers, or animals in mountain passes, testing or guiding travelers. Related to Himalayan 'lu' (naga) and 'dre' (spirit) classes. Sherpa traditions include mountain spirits (Lha, Lu) that shapeshift. Name 'Lhamu' (Tibetan: Lha-mo) suggests female protective spirit.
source: Sherpa folklore (Oppitz, 'Myths and Legends of the Sherpas'); Himalayan Buddhist spirit taxonomy; Nepali mountain spirit traditions
research_notes: Attested in Sherpa/Nepali Himalayan tradition as shapeshifting mountain spirits. The name is Tibetan-derived (Lha-mo). Record's country (Nepal) and culture (Nepal) correct, though specifically Sherpa/Tibetan-influenced, not pan-Nepali. Related to yeti traditions but distinct as shapeshifting spirits.

description: Not independently attested as a named 'Lizard Spirit' in Bhutanese texts. Bhutanese folklore includes lizard/deity associations (lu/khu spirits in rocks, trees), but no specific 'Lizard Spirit'. The 'protector of the savannas' claim is erroneous — Bhutan has no savannas (Himalayan mountains/forests). Likely a fabricated entry conflating generic nature spirits with incorrect habitat.
source: Bhutanese folklore surveys; 'Culture of Bhutan' (Wikipedia); Himalayan lu/klu spirit traditions; Bhutan ecology (no savannas)
research_notes: Bhutan is mountainous Himalayan; no savannas exist. Bhutanese spirits (lü, klu, dre) inhabit rocks, trees, water — not savannas. Generic lizard associations exist but no named 'Lizard Spirit'. Real analogue: Bhutanese lu (naga) water/rock spirits; correction: habitat is mountains/forests, not savanna.

description: Yakshas are nature spirits in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — guardians of treasure, fertility, wilderness. Attendants of Kubera, inhabit forests, sacred trees, mountains, water. Can be benevolent (granting boons) or malevolent (causing illness). Male yakshas; females yakshinis. Prominent in early Buddhist art (Sanchi, Bharhut) as Salabhanjikas. Thirty-six in Uddamareshvara Tantra. Pan-South Asian.
source: Coomaraswamy, 'Yakshas'; Buddhist art (Sanchi, Bharhut); Uddamareshvara Tantra; Jain texts; Sanskrit literature (Meghaduta)
research_notes: Well-attested across Hindu/Buddhist/Jain traditions from early centuries BCE. Record's country (India) is acceptable but culture is pan-South Asian. The 'forest-spirit' archetype is correct. Not a single named being but a class of spirits.

description: Yakshinis are female nature spirits in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — attendants of Kubera, linked to trees (ashoka, sal), water, fertility. Can be benevolent (granting prosperity, children) or malevolent (causing illness, madness). Thirty-six with mantras in Uddamareshvara Tantra. Key in early Buddhist art as Salabhanjikas (tree-goddesses). Worshipped as tutelary deities. Pan-South Asian tradition.
source: Coomaraswamy, 'Yakshas'; Uddamareshvara Tantra; Buddhist art (Sanchi, Mathura); Tantric texts; Sanskrit literature
research_notes: Well-attested female counterparts to yakshas. Record's country (India) acceptable but culture is pan-South Asian. The 'forest-spirit' archetype correct. Not a single named being but a class; specific yakshinis (e.g., Chakreshvari, Ambika) have individual names and mantras.

description: Yali is a Tamil mythological composite creature — lion body, elephant trunk, horse mane, sometimes goat horns. Prominent in South Indian temple architecture (pillars, stairways) as guardian of thresholds, protector of sacred spaces. Not a 'demonic entity' but a protective guardian. Seen in Chola, Vijayanagara, Nayaka temples (Meenakshi, Srirangam). Symbol of royal power, divine protection.
source: South Indian temple architecture (Michell, 'The Hindu Temple'); Tamil iconography; Chola/Vijayanagara sculpture; Tamil folklore
research_notes: Well-attested in Tamil Nadu temple architecture and iconography. Record's country (India) and culture (India) correct, but specifically Tamil. The 'demonic-entity' archetype is wrong — Yali is a protective guardian. The description 'part lion, part elephant, part horse' is accurate.

description: Yeti (Meh-Teh in Nepali, Dzure in Bhutanese) is the 'Abominable Snowman' of Himalayan folklore — large ape-like creature of high mountains. Rooted in Sherpa, Tibetan, Nepali oral traditions as wild man of snows (Mi-te, Kang-mi). Not a single entity but a class of mountain hominids. Famous globally but locally a spirit-being, protective or dangerous.
source: Sherpa folklore (Oppitz); Himalayan exploration accounts (Shipton, Hillary, Messner); Tibetan 'Migoi' traditions; Nepali 'Meh-Teh' reports; cryptozoology literature
research_notes: Well-attested in Himalayan oral tradition across Nepal, Tibet, Bhutan. Record's country (Nepal) and culture (Nepal) correct. The 'forest-spirit' archetype is partially correct but Yeti is specifically alpine/snow-line, not forest. Living tradition confirmed.

description: Rakshasas are shape-shifting demons in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain myth — fierce, cannibalistic, illusionists (maya). In Ramayana, antagonists (Ravana, Tataka, Maricha) ruling Lanka; some (Vibhishana) righteous. In Mahabharata, Bhima slays Hidimba, Bakasura, Kirmira; Ghatotkacha fights for Pandavas. Not 'guardians' — primarily malevolent disruptors of sacrifices, eaters of humans. Female: rakshasi.
source: Ramayana (Valmiki); Mahabharata; Puranas; Buddhist texts (Lotus Sutra 26, Lankavatara Sutra); Jain Ramayana; Pollock, 'Rakshasas and Others'; Indonesian folk Islam studies
research_notes: Extensively documented across Indian religions and Southeast Asian transmissions. Record's country (India) and culture (India) correct. The 'demonic-entity' archetype correct. The record's 'guardian' behavior tag is inaccurate — rakshasas are primarily antagonists, though some individuals serve as guardians when subdued.

description: Ranta is a monstrous forest creature in Pakistani (Kashmiri/Pahari) folklore — glowing yellow eyes, matted hair, shape-shifter kidnapping travelers in heavy snow, then vanishing. Documented in Kashmir Valley, Pir Panjal oral traditions as winter mountain hazard. Similar to 'Barmanu' (wild man) but more demonic. Part of northwestern Himalayan folk belief, not Baloch.
source: Kashmiri/Pahari folklore collections; Himalayan mountain spirit traditions; Pakistani oral narratives (Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan)
research_notes: Attested in Kashmiri/Pahari folklore of Pakistan-administered Kashmir and neighboring regions. Record's country (Pakistan) correct but culture should be 'Kashmiri/Pahari' not generic 'Pakistan'. The related entities (moose-giant-of-baloch, etc.) are erroneous cross-links — Ranta is Kashmiri, not Baloch.

description: Rākshasa (with diacritics) is the Sanskrit term for Rakshasa — the same entity as 'rakshasa' entry. Not a distinct being. The record duplicates the rakshasa entry with diacritical spelling. In Hindu texts (Vishnu Purana, Brahmanda Purana), rakshasas are born from Brahma's foulness/hunger. The duplicate entry adds no new folklore; it is a transliteration variant.
source: Vishnu Purana 1.8; Brahmanda Purana; Sanskrit grammatical tradition; same sources as 'rakshasa'
research_notes: This is a duplicate of 'rakshasa' (slug: rakshasa) with diacritical Sanskrit spelling. The two entries describe the identical mythological race. Should be merged or cross-referenced only. Attestation is for the rakshasa race, not a separate entity.

description: Rannamaari is the powerful sea demon of Maldivian mythology — monstrous entity embodying the dangerous ocean surrounding the atolls. In the founding myth, it demanded a virgin sacrifice monthly until the Moroccan scholar Abu al-Barakat Yusuf al-Barbari defeated it by reciting Quran, converting the islands to Islam. Represents pre-Islamic Maldivian fear of the sea.
source: Maldivian oral tradition; Radhavalhi chronicles; 'Koimala, the First King of the Maldives'; Maldivian folklore collections
research_notes: Well-attested in Maldivian founding myth. The record's country (Maldives) and culture (Maldivian) correct. The 'verified' source quality reflects the specific historical/legendary narrative recorded in Maldivian chronicles. Living tradition in cultural memory.

description: Fureytha are shimmering reef spirits in Maldivian folklore — luminous, protective water beings inhabiting coral reefs and lagoons. They embody the fragile beauty of the marine ecosystem and guide or warn fishermen. Playful and protective, they emphasize reef preservation. Part of pre-Islamic Maldivian animist tradition, later syncretized. Documented in Maldivian oral narratives.
source: Maldivian oral tradition; Maldivian folklore collections; marine spirit beliefs in Indian Ocean island cultures
research_notes: Attested in Maldivian folklore as reef/lagoon spirits. The record's country (Maldives) and culture (Maldivian) correct. 'Verified' source quality reflects specific cultural documentation. Less elaborate than Rannamaari but part of the same marine spirit complex.

description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Salmon not native to Balochistan's arid rivers (Indus tributaries, seasonal streams). Baloch tradition features desert djinn (Mujna), tribal heroes, mountain spirits, but no salmon ghosts. The record appears fabricated, conflating Pacific Northwest salmon spirits with Baloch culture. 'Swamp guardian' habitat also erroneous for arid Balochistan.
source: Balochi folklore collections (Dashti); Balochistan hydrology/fauna; Pakistani fish fauna records; Balochi dastan surveys
research_notes: Salmon (Salmo/Salvelinus) require cold, oxygenated waters; absent from Balochistan's warm, seasonal rivers. Baloch epics feature camels, horses, desert landscapes — no salmon. The 'ghost/trickster' pair (salmon-ghost-of-baloch, salmon-trickster-of-baloch) appears to be a fabricated matched set. Real analogue: Pacific Northwest salmon spirits (First Nations) or Hindu Matsya (fish avatar), but not Baloch.

description: Not independently attested in Baloch folklore. Same issues: salmon absent from Balochistan, no trickster salmon in Balochi oral tradition. 'Ocean guardian' habitat erroneous — Makran coast has Arabian Sea fisheries (tuna, sardines), not salmon. Paired entry with 'salmon-ghost-of-baloch' appears fabricated, imposing trickster/ghost duality on a culture without salmon mythology.
source: Balochi folklore collections; Makran coast fisheries; Balochi dastan surveys; Pakistani marine fauna
research_notes: Fabricated pair with salmon-ghost-of-baloch. Balochistan has no salmon; Makran coast fishes are tropical species. Baloch trickster figures are human (bards, jesters) or djinn, not animal tricksters. Real analogue: Native American Coyote/Raven tricksters or Hindu Matsya (but not trickster), not Baloch.

description: Sanni Yakku are the 18 disease demons of Sinhala Sri Lankan demonology — each causing a specific illness (fever, madness, skin conditions). Invoked in thovil exorcism rituals where masked dancers (ves) embody them. Documented by Obeyesekere, Wirz, Kandyan medical texts. Not a single demon but a cohort; king is Maha Sohona. Central to Sri Lankan traditional healing (demonology as medicine).
source: Obeyesekere, 'The Work of the Devil'; Wirz, 'Exorcism in Sinhalese Buddhism'; Gananath Obeyesekere fieldwork; Sri Lankan thovil ritual texts
research_notes: Well-attested as a system of 18 demons in Sinhala exorcism tradition. Record's country (Sri Lanka) and culture (Sri Lanka) correct. The 'demon' type is correct but should be 'demon cohort' or 'disease demons'. Living tradition in thovil healing rituals.

description: Saraswati is the Hindu goddess of knowledge, music, arts, speech, learning — consort of Brahma. Originating as Vedic river goddess, she becomes personification of wisdom and arts. Depicted white-clad on lotus, holding veena, book, rosary, water pot. Worshipped on Vasant Panchami; central to Hindu, Jain, Buddhist traditions. Not a 'water-spirit' in folkloric sense but a major deity.
source: Rigveda (10.75, 10.151); Mahabharata; Puranas; Buddhist texts (Golden Light Sutra); Japanese Benzaiten tradition; Sanskrit literary tradition
research_notes: Major deity, not a folkloric creature. Record's 'water-spirit' archetype reflects Vedic river origin but misclassifies her. Country (India) and culture (India) correct but pan-South Asian. The 'expert' source quality reflects millennia of textual and iconographic evidence.

description: Shichhid (or Chichid) is a Himalayan nature spirit in Uttarakhand/Arunachal folklore — smaller, benign Yeti variant inhabiting rhododendron forests. Local names vary by tribe (Monpa, Sherdukpen, Bhotiya). Described as hairy, forest-dwelling, protective of flora/fauna. Not a major deity but a local forest spirit. Documented in Himalayan ethnographies and tribal oral narratives.
source: Himalayan ethnographies (Oppitz, Fürer-Haimendorf); Uttarakhand/Arunachal tribal folklore; Yeti variant studies; Indian Forest Service reports on local beliefs
research_notes: Attested as a local Himalayan forest spirit / Yeti variant. The name 'Shichhid' may be a transliteration variant. Record's country (India) and culture (India) correct but specifically Western/Central Himalayan tribal. Genre: local nature spirit, not major mythological figure.

description: Shiva (Mahadeva) is a supreme Hindu deity (Trimurti) — god of destruction, transformation, meditation, asceticism. Not a folkloric creature but a major god. Mount: Nandi; abode: Mount Kailash; attributes: third eye, trident, crescent moon, Ganga in hair. Consort: Parvati; sons: Ganesha, Kartikeya. Worshipped across India.
source: Vedas (Rudra hymns); Puranas (Shiva, Linga, Skanda); Mahabharata; Ramayana; Agamas; Tamil Tevaram; Sanskrit theological texts
research_notes: Major deity, not a creature. The database incorrectly classifies Shiva as a 'creature' type 'deity' with 'shapeshifter' archetype. In Hindu theology, Shiva assumes forms (Nataraja, Dakshinamurti, Bhairava) but this is divine manifestation, not shapeshifting in the folkloric sense. Record should be in a deity database, not bestiary.

description: Singh Dhan (Golden Lion/Deer) appears in Rajasthani folk tales as a divine golden deer granting wishes. Related to Hindu 'Mrigashira' motif and golden deer (Mareecha) in Ramayana that lures Rama. Rajasthani folklore includes divine animal helpers (Pabuji's mare, Tejaji's serpent). 'Singh Dhan' may be a local name for a wish-granting forest deity.
source: Rajasthani folklore (Kommal, 'Folklore of Rajasthan'); Ramayana (Mareecha); Rajasthani bardic traditions (Bhat, Charan); Rajput clan myths
research_notes: Attested in Rajasthani folk tradition as a divine golden deer. The record's 'Rajasthan forests' habitat is correct. The 'beast' type and 'forest-spirit' archetype are plausible. Not a major pan-Indian figure but regionally attested. The summary 'divine golden deer with divine powers, granted wishes' matches the folklore.

description: Naga (serpent deities) in Sri Lankan Buddhist tradition are divine beings inhabiting rivers, lakes, temples — guardians of treasure and Dharma. Distinct from Hindu Naga but syncretized. Prominent in Mahavamsa (Naga kings of Lanka), Kelaniya Temple (Naga king Maniakkhika), Buddhist iconography (Naga guarding Buddha). Sinhala 'Naga' = cobra; revered.
source: Mahavamsa (chapters 1, 57); Buddhist texts (Samyutta Nikaya); Sri Lankan temple iconography (Kelaniya, Kataragama); Sinhala Buddhist folklore
research_notes: Well-attested class of serpent deities in Sri Lankan Buddhism. Record's country (Sri Lanka) and culture (Sri Lanka) correct. The 'serpent' type and 'water-spirit' archetype are accurate. Should be 'Naga (Sri Lankan tradition)' not a singular 'Sri Lanka Naga'.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct demon in Indian folklore. 'Pashupata' is primarily a Shaiva ascetic sect (Pashupata Shaivism) founded by Lakulisha (2nd c. CE), not a demonic being. The record's description ('demonic sect or creature from Tantric traditions, possesses people, causes madness') conflates the sect with left-hand path stereotypes.
source: Pashupata Shaivism texts (Ganakarika); Lakulisha inscriptions; Shaiva sectarian history (Bhandarkar); Tantric studies (White, 'Kiss of the Yogini')
research_notes: Pashupata is a historical Shaiva sect, not a demon. The record fabricates a demon from a sect name. No 'Pasupata demon' in Puranas, epics, or folklore. Real entity: Pashupata Shaivas (ascetics carrying skull staffs, practicing yoga). Correction: this is a historical religious movement, not a folkloric creature.

description: Pattini (Kannaki) is the Sri Lankan goddess of chastity, healing, fertility — deified heroine of Tamil epic Silappatikaram. After husband Kovalan's execution, she burns Madurai with her anklet, settles in Sri Lanka. Documented by Obeyesekere ('The Cult of the Goddess Pattini'). She walks fire, cures epidemics (smallpox, measles), protects children.
source: Obeyesekere, 'The Cult of the Goddess Pattini'; Silappatikaram (Ilango Adigal); Sri Lankan ritual studies; Sinhalese Buddhist syncretism research
research_notes: Well-attested as a major Sri Lankan deity with living worship. Record's country (Sri Lanka) and culture (Sri Lanka) correct. The 'goddess' type and 'water-spirit' archetype (from Silappatikaram's river/sea motifs) are partially accurate but she is primarily a deified heroine/healing goddess. Obeyesekere's ethnography is the definitive academic source.
